analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover three primary care and three mental health visits with no copays or deductibles.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in any of the three committees it was sent to, and the two-year Congress ended without the House taking it up.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal health insurance rules to require group health plans and insurers selling group or individual coverage to pay for three primary care visits and three behavioral health visits each year with no cost sharing — no copay, no deductible. It also defines which providers count, forbids plans from limiting those visits more tightly than other covered visits, and requires the same payment rates as for any other visit. It was referred to three House committees in January 2020 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private insurance who skip doctor visits or mental health care because of copays and deductibles. The bill's text makes the first three primary care and three behavioral health visits each plan year free, and a separate provision lets high-deductible health plans pay for these visits before the deductible [S3]. The bill's sponsor introduced it in January 2020 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who skip care over copays

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and group and individual insurance to cover three primary care visits and three behavioral health visits per plan year with no cost sharing [S2][S3].
Bars plans from imposing treatment limitations on those six visits that are stricter than those for other covered visits, and requires the same reimbursement rates as for comparable visits [S3].
Changes the tax code definition of high-deductible health plans so they may cover these visits before the deductible is met, protecting people with deductible-only plans [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and self-insured employers pay for the six free visits per member per year, likely through modestly higher premiums. Primary care and behavioral health providers would see more visits but be paid the same rates as comparable visits.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is unfunded: insurers and self-insured employers would bear the added cost, which would likely show up as higher premiums spread across all enrollees, including people who never use the visits.
Six visits a year is a narrow benefit — people with chronic conditions or ongoing mental health treatment would still owe cost sharing after the third visit [S3].
The bill does not direct funding to expand the supply of primary care or behavioral health clinicians, so added demand could strain provider networks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: free early access to a doctor and to mental health care catches problems cheaply and removes the deductible barrier that keeps many people — especially those in high-deductible plans — from seeking care at all. The cost is small relative to total premiums and would be spread broadly. The main weakness is the narrow scope of six visits, which helps people at the margin more than people needing ongoing treatment.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees in January 2020 and sat there; none scheduled a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Lauren Underwood, joined by Rep. Kim Schrier, introduced the bill on January 10, 2020 [S3][S5].
It was referred to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote; the bill died when the 116th Congress ended [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and self-insured employers are better off because no new free-visit requirement was ever imposed; people facing copays and deductibles gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Lauren Underwood
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Primary and Behavioral Health Care Access Act of 2020 in the House.

for.name: 20 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 20 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House committee leadership (Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Ways and Means)
against.role: Chairs controlling whether the bill got a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled any action on the bill after referral; it received no hearing, markup, or vote in the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only the bill's fate split the record: all 20 cosponsors were Democrats, and no member or bloc ever voted on the bill, so no partisan opposition was ever put on the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would force insurers to pay for six visits per member per year without cost sharing, cutting into arrangements where copays and deductibles hold down their claims costs. Because the bill died in committee, insurers never had to change anything.

industries.industry: Self-insured employers and employer benefit plans
industries.note: ERISA plans are directly covered by the bill, so large employers running their own health plans would have absorbed the cost of the six free visits. The bill's death leaves the current cost-sharing structure untouched.

industries.industry: Primary care and behavioral health providers
industries.note: Removing cost sharing on the first three visits of each type would bring in patients who currently skip care over copays and deductibles. The bill requires the same reimbursement rates as comparable visits, so payment would not be cut.
